Let Γ;s be an extended context.
Let t₀, t₁ and t₂ be terms.
If Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁ and Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≤ t₂
then for all extended context Γ′;s′ with Γ;s ↣ Γ′;s′,
there exists a term t₃,
such that Γ;s ⊢ t₂ ⟶≡ t₃ and Γ′;s′ ⊢ t₁ ⟶≤ t₃.
Diagrammatically, where the solid arrows are the conditions for the existence of the dashed arrows.
t₂ t₃ t₀ t₁ ≡ ≡ ≤ ≤
Proof.
By induction on the term structure of t₀.
We consider cases according to the last
two rules that are applied respectively in the derivation of the horizontal and
vertical edges of the diagram above, starting by the bottom-left corner.
The cases where bottom rule is rule Me-Top or respectively rule Me-TAp,
then the missing top edge is by rule Me-Top or respectively Me-TAp,
and the missing right edge is by rule Ms-Top.
If the vertical edge rule is Ms-Top,
then the missing top edge is by rule Me-Top,
and the missing right edge is by rule Ms-Top.
If the vertical edge is Ms-Equ, then we have
Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁ and Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₂.
By reflexivity of ⟶≡ (Proposition 18), we have
Γ;s ↣ Γ;s.
Hence by Lemma 2 we have
Γ;s ⊢ t₂ ⟶≡ t₃ and Γ′;s′ ⊢ t₁ ⟶≡ t₃.
Thanks to rule Ms-Equ, from the latter derivation, we obtain Γ′;s′ ⊢ t₁ ⟶≤ t₃.
We know that if the rule Me-Pro appears in the derivation tree Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≤ t₂,
then we have in fact Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₂, and as a result the results follows from
Lemma 2 as outlined by the paragraph outlined above.
We therefore assume that the rule Me-Pro doesn’t appear in the derivation tree Γ;s ⊢ t₀ ⟶≤ t₂,
an information useful only for the last case of this lemma.
Else, for the general case we distinguish the sub-cases below:
Case Me-Pro with Ms-Pro:
We need to prove the diagram below:
By assumption, we have the following reductions:
Γ;s ⊢ x ⟶≡ α′ with x ≡ α∈Γ
Γ;s ⊢ x ⟶≤ t₂ with x ≤ t∈Γ
By prevalidity of the context, we cannot have two distinct annotation for x in the context,
and therefore this case is impossible: there cannot be a subtype annotation and an equivalence
annotation in the prevalid context Γ.
Case Me-Var with Ms-Pro:
We need to prove the diagram below:
By assumption, we have the following reductions:
Γ;s ⊢ x ⟶≡ x.
Γ;s ⊢ x ⟶≤ t by rule Ms-Pro.
From rule Ms-Pro, we know there exists an annotation x ≤ t∈Γ.
Let Γ=Γ₀,x ≤ t,Γ₁ for some context parts Γ₀ and Γ₁.
Let Γ′;s′ be an extended context such that Γ;s ↣ Γ′;s′.
By Lemma 36, we obtain Γ;nil ↣ Γ′;nil
from Γ;s ↣ Γ′;s′.

Γ,x ≤ t₀;nil ⊢ u₀ ⟶≤ u₂

Because in our case s=nil, we have s′=nil.
By rule Ct-Ann, we have Γ,x ≤ t₀;nil ↣ Γ′,x ≤ t₁;nil
from Γ;nil ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁.
By induction hypothesis on u₀, there exists a term u₃ such that:

Γ′,x ≤ t₁;nil ⊢ u₁ ⟶≤ u₃

Case Me-FOp with Ms-FOp:
We need to prove the diagram below:
{λ x ≤ t₀.u₂}. {λ x ≤ t₀.u₀} {λ x ≤ t₁.u₁} ≡ ≤ ≡ ≤

Γ;α::s ⊢ λ x ≤ t₀.u₀ ⟶≡ λ x ≤ t₁.u₁ by Me-FOp, which gives us:

Γ;α::s ⊢ λ x ≤ t₀.u₀ ⟶≤ λ x ≤ t₀.u₂ by Ms-FOp, which gives us:
Γ,x ≡ α;s ⊢ u₀ ⟶≤ u₂
Let Γ′;s′ be an extended context such that Γ;s ↣ Γ′;s′.
In our case, we have s=α::s₀ and s′=α′::s₁ with by rule Ct-Stk, Γ;nil ⊢ α ⟶≡ α′.
By rule Ct-Stk, we have Γ;s₀ ↣ Γ′;s₁

from Γ;s ↣ Γ′;s′.
We now have Γ,x ≡ α;s₀ ↣ Γ′,x ≡ α′;s₁ by rule Ct-Ann.
By induction hypothesis on u₀, there exists a term u₃ such that:
Γ,x ≡ α;s₀ ⊢ u₂ ⟶≡ u₃
Γ′,x ≡ α′;s₁ ⊢ u₁ ⟶≤ u₃
We now have
Γ;α::s₀ ⊢ λ x ≤ t₀.u₂ ⟶≡ λ x ≤ t₁.u₃ by Me-FOp
from Γ;nil ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁ and Γ,x ≡ α;s₀ ⊢ u₂ ⟶≡ u₃

from Γ′,x ≡ α′;s₁ ⊢ u₁ ⟶≤ u₃

Lemma 2 ( ⟶≡ has the diamond property).
Let Γ₀;s₀ be an extended context.
Let t₀, t₁, and t₂ be terms.
If Γ₀;s₀ ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁ and Γ₀;s₀ ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₂,
then for any extended contexts
Γ₁;s₁ and Γ₂;s₂ such that Γ₀;s₀ ↣ Γ₁;s₁ and Γ₀;s₀ ↣ Γ₂;s₂,
there exists a term t₃
such that Γ₁;s₁ ⊢ t₁ ⟶≡ t₃ and Γ₂;s₂ ⊢ t₂ ⟶≡ t₃.
Moreover, for any variable x, if in the derivation of Γ₀;s₀ ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁
(respectively Γ₀;s₀ ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₂ )
there isn’t an application of the Rule Me-Pro that makes a promotion of variable x,
then in the derivation Γ₂;s₂ ⊢ t₂ ⟶≡ t₃
(respectively Γ₁;s₁ ⊢ t₁ ⟶≡ t₃ )
there won’t be an application of the Rule Me-Pro that makes a promotion of variable x.

We now proceed by induction on the derivation tree of Γ₀;s₀ ⊢ t₀ ⟶≡ t₁.

two rules that are applied respectively in the derivation of the horizontal and
vertical edges of the diagram above, starting by the bottom-left corner. The base case
corresponds to when these two rules are both Me-Top (respectively both Me-Var),
for which the lemma holds by using the rule Me-Top (respectively Me-Var) for the missing edges.

Theorem 3 ensures that the transitivity step

Our constructive proof produces a transitivity-free derivation of
Γ;nil ⊢ A a ≤* A a (i.e., flattens it into
Γ;nil ⊢ A a ≤ A a witnessed by the straight vertical
and horizontal paths in the middle of the diagram), and then applies the commutativity
theorem to complete the upper-right corner of the diagram, obtaining the transitivity-free

in our algorithmic system thanks to the operand stack and Rule Ms-FOp which
exposes the term (λ x ≤ A.a) a, and to the fact that the derivation

middle of the diagram preserves the possibly convoluted derivation
Γ,x ≡ a;nil ⊢ a ≤* A as a sub-derivation (marked with
). Although preserving this convoluted derivation seems at first glance
counter-intuitive, it gives the opportunity to apply the induction hypothesis of the
Theorem 3 to the term
(λ x ≤ A.a) a, which will flatten the convoluted derivation. Contrary to
ours, Hutchins’ attempts at proving that transitivity is admissible reduce the complexity
of the intermediate step by avoiding the convoluted derivation upfront (by directly taking
the reduction (λ x ≤ A.x) a ⟶≤ (λ x ≤ A.A) a which
promotes the formal parameter a of the redex to its annotation A ).
But this premature promotion of a formal parameter to its type annotation is in fact
counter-productive, which manifests in the failure of Hutchins’ proof of the commutativity
theorem, where the premature promotion prevents one from completing the diagram for
redexes with a transitivity-free right edge.
This result was the missing cornerstone in Hutchins’ original theory, and its proof here
is necessary for establishing type safety. In the next section, we present what can be a
type-safe theory based on our MPSS.
4 Towards a Type-Safe System
Thanks to the above commutative system, we can now sketch the design of a type-safe
system. The static semantics for this system is defined by a well-formedness
judgment, presented in Figure 4, which is the static
condition for type safety. Rules Wf-PrS and Wf-PrE ensure that a
variable is well-formed if and only if it occurs in a prevalid context (respectively, in a
subtype or an equivalence annotation). Rule Wf-Top ensures that ⊤ is
universally well-formed. Rule Wf-Fun ensures that an abstraction is well-formed
if and only if it has a well-formed annotation, and its body is well-formed in a context
enlarged with the abstraction annotation. Finally, Rule Wf-App ensures that an
application is well-formed if and only if it has an operator that is a well-subtype of a
function, and an operand that is a well-subtype of the operator’s subtype annotation.

static system to our dynamic reduction semantics. For example, Rule Ws-Lf2 states

5 Related work
PSS naturally subsumes dependent types and higher-order subtyping, so we comment on both
ideas.
There are many works related to dependent types. For instance in Cayenne
[4], Idris [7] or Haskell
[21], dependent types are an extension of the language, in contrast to
our case where dependent types are built-in as there is no distinction between terms and
types.
Other languages mainly use dependent types for theorem proving, for instance Coq
[12] or Agda [6]. Our language is not strongly normalising,
and our main goal is not theorem proving as we cannot use the language as a proof system,
since applying the Curry-Howard correspondence to PSS in a consistent way is still an open
question.
To accommodate the Curry-Howard correspondence, one possible approach is to distinguish
between potentially non-terminating terms and terminating terms, either with monads or via
other means [23, 24]. λ^ is a
calculus that explores this idea
combines proofs and programs into a single language that distinguishes two fragments, a
logical fragment where every term is strongly normalising that is suited to write proofs,
and a programmatic fragment that is Turing complete and lacks termination. Such systems
allow so-called freedom of speech, which is the ability to write (terminating)
proofs about non-terminating terms.
Subtyping extensions of type systems have been considered. In 1997, Chen proposed
λ_C_≤ [11], an extension of the calculus of constructions
λ_C with subtyping. However, Chen’s λ_C_≤ supports neither top types
nor bounded quantification as we do in PSS.
Various extensions of System F, in order to equip it with subtyping, have also been
considered in the literature. Within these we find System F ≤
[8] and System F _≤^ [25], which
respectively add subtyping and higher-order subtyping capabilities. PSS subsumes the
version of System F ≤ without contravariant arrow-types [18].
The origin of mixing terms and types goes back to the introduction of pure type systems
[22], which generalises the seminal works on lambda calculi with types
by [5]. These systems have the ability to unify types and terms under the same
kind, but there is a typing relation instead of a subtyping one. Moreover, in some of
these pure type systems, the type is inhabited. This gives rise to the well-known
Girard’s paradox (see [17]). In our system, there is not a
primitive subtype, but we could encode such a subtype to be inhabited by itself,
and that would be unproblematic since our aim is not to use PSS as a theorem prover.
Systems where terms can be used in certain ways as types have been considered. Aspinall
studied the combination of subtyping with singleton types
[3]. Singleton types are close to what we study, as in our
calculus, terms can be seen as singleton types of this unique value. We have for instance,
for every term t, ε⊢ t ≤ t, which would be translated to
⊢ t:\ in a system with singleton types.
Other attempts to unify typing and subtyping exist. A more conservative attempt that tries
to unify typing and subtyping is [31]. This work has two major
differences with our approach. First, in [31] the subtyping relation
still tracks types (their unification of subtyping and typing is more conservative than
ours). Second, in PSS functions and function (sub)types are defined with the same syntax,

Because many interesting features described in [18] are related to
modules, other type systems especially related to objects have been studied. Our work
shares foundational goals with the Dependent Object Types (DOT) calculus, the theoretical
basis for Scala 3 [2, 27]. Both PSS and DOT aim to create
powerful, unified type systems that support advanced modularity, and provide a formal

6 Future work
As described in Section 4, it is left as future work to define a type
system that is built upon MPSS and to prove its type safety. Another interesting area to
explore is the link between our system and Hutchins’ system, to determine if both
well-formed notions are equivalent.
Once this system is defined, it is also left as future work to obtain an algorithm that
typechecks terms in MPSS. Hutchins describes an algorithm for his system in
[18], but one should adapt his algorithm to this new system, and study
upon which conditions it terminates. One possible approach is to use the operational
relevance of terms, for which there exist some arguments that lead them to terminate. We
leave as future work to explore other practical algorithms which terminate on
operationally relevant terms.
Another venue of future work is to study whether PSS and MPSS are Turing-complete. To the
best of our knowledge, whether PSS is Turing-complete has not been formally proven yet.
The argument in favor of Turing-completeness rests on the existence of a (well-formed)
looping combinator in PSS, which would consist of a family of terms L_n such that
L_n f β -reduces to f(L_n+1 f) for any f. Such a looping combinator
exists for System  λ* [16], which can be encoded into Hutchins’ PSS
thanks to the encoding of System  λ* in Hutchins’ PSS, provided on page 47 of
[18]. In order to establish Turing-completeness of PSS, one should now
adapt the argument made by [14] in Section 2 or the argument made in
[15]. There is, however, no simple known expression of a looping combinator in
System  λ*. The looping combinator from [16] can only be derived
mechanically, and working with it directly is proven to be hard as its length is more than
40 pages (see the discussion on the logical consistency and impredicativity of
System  λ_◁ on pages 48–51 of [18]). It may therefore be
difficult to conclude about Turing-completeness of either PSS or MPSS, which is left as
future work.
7 Conclusion
This paper presents a variant of the PSS originally introduced by Hutchins in
[18], which we name MPSS, and proves that our reformulation enjoys a key
commutation property which was missing in Hutchins’ system. We also sketch how a type
system can be derived from MPSS, which could lead to a type-safe system. To the best of
our knowledge PSS and MPSS are the first theories that unify harmoniously terms and types
by using a single kind where everything is a subtype.
Meta-theories of languages with advanced features on types are notoriously difficult to
work with. We believe our work could help in laying the foundations for a new approach
that mixes terms and types in innovative ways.

paper: Lemma 9.
Let Γ;s be an extended context, and Γ′ be a logical context,
such that Γ,Γ′[x\α];nil is prevalid.
Let u, v, t and α be terms, such that
both u[x\α] and v[x\α] are well-formed in context Γ,Γ′[x\α].
If Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v,
and Γ ⊢ α≤*wf t.
Then Γ,Γ′[x\α]⊢ u[x\α]≤*wf v[x\α].
Proof.
In this lemma, we have two cases, either the derivation Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v
depending on if our derivation is of the form Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ Co[x]⟶≤ Co[t] for some covariant context Co.
If it is:
By assumption, we have both u[x\α] and v[x\α] well-formed in context Γ,Γ′[x\α],
because the derivation Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v
is Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ Co[x]⟶≤ Co[t],
these terms are Co_[x\α][α] and Co_[x\α][t].
From Γ ⊢ α≤*wf t we have by weakening (Lemma 19)
Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α]⊢ α≤*wf t.
We therefore have Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α]⊢ α≤*wf t,
and both Co_[x\α][α] and Co_[x\α][t] well-formed in Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α].
Hence by Conjecture 8, we obtain
Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α]⊢ Co_[x\α][α]≤*wf Co_[x\α][t].
Because there is no instance of the variable x in neither α nor in t,
this last derivation is
Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α]⊢ u[x\α]≤*wf v[x\α].
By prevalidity of Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′[x\α], we know that there is no instance of the variable x
in Γ. As a result, there is no instance of this variable anywhere.
As a result, we have
Γ,Γ′[x\α]⊢ u[x\α]≤*wf v[x\α] the desired result.
Else:
We apply Lemma 30 to obtain
Γ,Γ′[x\α];nil ⊢ u[x\α]⟶≤ v[x\α].
By rule Ws-Rfl, we have
Γ,Γ′[x\α]⊢ v[x\α]≤wf v[x\α].
Hence, by rule Ws-Lft,
Γ,Γ′[x\α]⊢ u[x\α]≤wf v[x\α].
Because both terms are well-formed by assumption, we have by rule Ws-Sub,
Γ,Γ′[x\α]⊢ u[x\α]≤*wf v[x\α]
the desired result.

paper: Lemma 10 (Inversion lemma.).
Let Γ be a logical context.
Let λ x ≤ t.u and λ x ≤ t′.u′ be terms.
If Γ ⊢ (λ x ≤ t.u) ≤*wf (λ x ≤ t′.u′) then
Γ ⊢ t ≡wf t′.
Proof.
By induction on the number of transitivity step of
Γ ⊢ (λ x ≤ t.u) ≤*wf (λ x ≤ t′.u′),
we obtain Γ ⊢ (λ x ≤ t.u) ≤* (λ x ≤ t′.u′)
by applying Proposition 13 on each of these transitivity steps.
By transitivity elimination (Lemma 3), we then obtain
Γ;nil ⊢ (λ x ≤ t.u) ≤ (λ x ≤ t′.u′).
By definition, there exists a term z such that
Γ;nil ⊢ (λ x ≤ t.u) ⟶≡↠ z and
Γ;nil ⊢ (λ x ≤ t′.u′) ⟶≤↠ z.
On the first derivation, based on the structure of the term λ x ≤ t.u,
only the rule Me-Fun can be applied, and therefore there exists a function
λ x ≤ t_z.u_z such that z=λ x ≤ t_z.u_z.
Because only the rule Me-Fun has been applied, we also have
Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ t_z.
We apply the same reasoning on the derivation Γ;nil ⊢ (λ x ≤ t′.u′) ⟶≤↠ z,
which consists only of use of the rule Ms-Fun or Ms-Equ with Me-Fun,
and therefore we have as well Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ t_z.
By rule Ws-Rfl, we have Γ ⊢ t_z ≡wf t_z.
We now show that we have Γ ⊢ t ≡wf t_z by induction on the number of derivation steps of
Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ t_z. If there is no derivation step, then we have t=t_z and the result holds.
Otherwise, there exists a term t′ such that Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′
and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ t_z. By the induction hypothesis on the number of derivation steps of
Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ t_z, we obtain Γ ⊢ t′ ≡wf t_z.
By rule Ws-Lf1 on Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′ and Γ ⊢ t′ ≡wf t_z,
we obtain Γ ⊢ t ≡wf t_z.
By the same reasoning on the number of derivation steps of Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ t_z,
we obtain Γ ⊢ t ≡ t′ from Γ ⊢ t ≡wf t_z and the rule Ws-Rgh.

paper: Theorem 11 (No supertype of Top.).
Let Γ;s be an extended context.
Let λ x ≤ t.u be a term. We cannot
have Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ≤* λ x ≤ t.u.
Proof.
First we transform Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ≤* λ x ≤ t.u
into Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ≤ λ x ≤ t.u by transitivity elimination (Lemma 3).
Assume towards a contradiction that
Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ≤ λ x ≤ t.u. By definition of the subtyping relation, there exists w
such that Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≤↠ w and Γ;s ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ⟶≡↠ w.
From Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≤↠ w, we obtain that w=⊤
since ⊤ can only promote to itself, with rules Ms-Equ and
Ms-Top. Now from Γ;s ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ⟶≡↠ w, we know that w is an
abstraction since the only rule for equivalence reduction that can be applied to
λ x ≤ t.u is rule Ms-Fun or Ms-FOp. But this contradicts the w=⊤ established
earlier and we are done.

paper: Proposition 12 (Well-formedness extraction).
Let Γ be an extended context and u and v be terms. If
Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v then both derivation Γ ⊢ u wf and
Γ ⊢ v wf exist in the derivation tree Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v.
Proof.
Note: the requirement that the derivation trees ( Γ ⊢ u wf and Γ ⊢ v wf )
exist in the original derivation tree is used on other lemmas because we do induction on derivation trees.
It is not enough to know that Γ ⊢ u wf and Γ ⊢ v wf exist,
they need to be a subtree of our original tree. Hence this formulation.
By induction on the derivation tree of Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v. If the last
rule applied is Ws-Sub, then the result holds from the assumption of the rule.
Else, the last rule applied is Wf-Trans, then there exists a term t such that
Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf t and Γ ⊢ t ≤*wf v, and the result
holds by the induction hypothesis.

paper: Proposition 13 (From well-subtyping to subtyping.).
Let Γ be a logical context and u and v be terms. If
Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v then Γ;nil ⊢ u ≤ v.
Proof.
By induction on the derivation tree of Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v.
We distinguish cases based on the last rule used in the derivation tree.
Rule Ws-Rfl:
In this case, we have u=v=t.
By Proposition 18, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t.
By rule Ms-Equ, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≤ t.
By definition of the subtype relation ≤, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ≤ t.
Rule Ws-Lf1 or Ws-Lf2:
In this case, we have as premises Γ ⊢ v′ ≤wf t,
By induction hypothesis, we obtain Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ≤ t.
By definition of ≤, there exists z such that Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ⟶≤↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ z.
The reduction Γ;nil ⊢ v{{◁}{}}v′ is
either Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′ or Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′.
In the former case, by rule Ms-Equ, we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′.
Hence we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′.
Hence Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤↠ v′.
We now have Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤↠ v′ and Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ⟶≤↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤↠ z.
By definition of ≤, we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ≤ t.
Rule Ws-Rgh:
In this case, we have as premises Γ ⊢ v ≤wf t′,
Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′.
By induction hypothesis, we obtain Γ;nil ⊢ v ≤ t′.
By definition of ≤, there exists z such that Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z.
By definition of ⟶≡, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≤ t′ and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≤ t.
Hence Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≤↠ t′.
We now have Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≤↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ z ⟶≤↠ t′.
We have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≤↠ t′ and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≤↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≤↠ z.
By definition of ≤, we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ≤ t.

paper: Proposition 14 (From well-equivalence to equivalence.).
Let Γ be a logical context and u and v be terms. If
Γ ⊢ u ≡wf v then Γ;nil ⊢ u ≡ v.
Proof.
By induction on the derivation tree of Γ ⊢ u ≡wf v.
We distinguish cases based on the last rule used in the derivation tree.
Rule Ws-Rfl:
In this case, we have u=v=t.
By Proposition 18, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t.
By rule Ms-Equ, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t.
By definition of the subtype relation ≡, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ≡ t.
Rule Ws-Lf1:
In this case, we have as premises Γ ⊢ v′ ≡wf t,
Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′.
By induction hypothesis, we obtain Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ≡ t.
By definition of ≡, there exists z such that Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ⟶≡↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ z.
From Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′ we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ v′.
We now have Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ v′ and Γ;nil ⊢ v′ ⟶≡↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ z.
By definition of ≡, we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ≡ t.
Rule Ws-Rgh:
In this case, we have as premises Γ ⊢ v ≡wf t′,
Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′.
By induction hypothesis, we obtain Γ;nil ⊢ v ≡ t′.
By definition of ≡, there exists z such that Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z.
By definition of ⟶≡, we have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′ and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡ t.
Hence Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ t′.
We now have Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z and Γ;nil ⊢ z ⟶≡↠ t′.
We have Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ t′ and Γ;nil ⊢ t′ ⟶≡↠ z, hence Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡↠ z.
By definition of ≡, we have Γ;nil ⊢ v ≡ t.

paper: Lemma 19 (Weakening of context).
Let Γ;s and Γ′;s′ be two extended contexts such that Γ,Γ′;s@s′ is prevalid.
Let u and v be terms.
We have the following relations:
If Γ ⊢ u wf then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u wf.
If Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤wf v.
If Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ≤ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤ v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ≤* v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤* v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v then Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
If Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v then Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v.
Proof.
Note: this lemma is a group of different lemmas which are proved separately.
This proof dispatches the proof of each of these lemmas to their respective proof.
We do a case disjunction based on the case we are in:
Case Γ ⊢ u wf or Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v or Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v :
Done in Lemma 20.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ≤ v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ≤ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤ v.
By definition of the relation ≤, there exists a term z such that
Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ z and Γ;s ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ z.
By using respectively Lemma 21 and Lemma 22
on respectively Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ z and Γ;s ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ z,
we respectively obtain Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ z and Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ v ⟶≡↠ z.
By definition of the relation ≤, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤ v.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ≤* v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ≤* v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤* v.
By definition of the relation ≤*,
there exists u₁,,u_n such that
Γ;s ⊢ u ≤ u₁, Γ;s ⊢ u₁ ≤ u₂,·s,Γ;s ⊢ u_n ≤ v.
By using the reasoning of the case above on each Γ;s ⊢ u_i ≤ u_i+1, we obtain
Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤ u₁, Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u₁ ≤ u₂,·s,Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u_n ≤ v.
By definition of the relation ≤*, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ≤* v.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v.
We proceed by induction on the derivation tree of Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ v.
The proof can be found in Lemma 21.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v then Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v.
By definition of the relation ⟶≤↠, there exists u₁,,u_n such that
Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ u₁, Γ;s ⊢ u₁ ⟶≤ u₂,·s,Γ;s ⊢ u_n ⟶≤ v.
By using Lemma 21 multiple times, we obtain
Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤ u₁, Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u₁ ⟶≤ u₂,·s,Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u_n ⟶≤ v.
By definition of the relation ⟶≤↠, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ v.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v then Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
We proceed by induction on the derivation tree of Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
The proof can be found in Lemma 22.
Case Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v :
We need to prove that if Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v then Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v.
By definition of the relation ⟶≡↠, there exists u₁,,u_n such that
Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ u₁, Γ;s ⊢ u₁ ⟶≡ u₂,·s,Γ;s ⊢ u_n ⟶≡ v.
By using Lemma 22 multiple times, we obtain
Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡ u₁, Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u₁ ⟶≡ u₂,·s,Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u_n ⟶≡ v.
By definition of the relation ⟶≡↠, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ v.
Lemma 20 (Weakening of context - Aux).
Let Γ and Γ′ be two logical contexts such that Γ,Γ′ is prevalid.
Let u and v be terms.
We have the following relations:
If Γ ⊢ u wf then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u wf.
If Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤wf v.
If Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v then Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf v.
Proof.
We need to prove all of these relations together, because any derivation tree of any of these relations
will contain a derivation tree of the other relations.
Consider for instance Γ ⊢ (λ x ≤ ⊤.x) ⊤ wf.
One of the premise of this derivation tree is Γ ⊢ ⊤ ≤*wf ⊤,
which will ultimately have as premise Γ ⊢ ⊤ ≤wf ⊤ and Γ ⊢ ⊤ wf.
The proof therefore consider all of these relations together.
The proof works by induction on the derivation tree,
for the example above for instance, Γ ⊢ ⊤ wf is considered a base case, and therefore
we have Γ,Γ′ ⊢ ⊤ wf, from which we will be able to conclude Γ,Γ′ ⊢ ⊤ ≤wf ⊤,
and so on.
Assume any of the cases of this lemma.
We do an induction on the size of the derivation tree of either
(Γ ⊢ u wf)₁, (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂ or (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃
which we index by i for i∈\1,2,3\ as a indexed family,
one of the three possible cases of this lemma.
The induction hypothesis can be called on any element of this family, as long as the size of its derivation tree
is smaller.
For instance, consider a derivation tree ending by the rule Wf-App
(for instance (Γ ⊢ u v wf)₁ ), its premises are
derivations of the form (Γ ⊢ v ≤*wf w)₃, on which we can apply the induction hypothesis
because their size are smaller despite not being in the same index.
Suppose we are now in the case 1, that is (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁, let’s prove (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u wf)₁.
We distinguish cases based on the last rule used in the derivation tree (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁.
Rule Wf-PrS or rule Wf-PrE with u=x :
In this case, we have x ◁ t∈Γ,
and therefore x ◁ t∈Γ∪Γ′.
By assumption, we have Γ,Γ′;s@s′ prevalid, hence Γ,Γ′ prevalid.
Hence by rule Wf-PrS or rule Wf-PrE, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ x wf.
Rule Wf-Top:
In this case, we have as premises Γ prevalid.
By assumption, we have Γ,Γ′;s@s′ prevalid, hence Γ,Γ′ prevalid.
We now have Γ,Γ′ ⊢ ⊤ wf by rule Wf-Top.
Rule Wf-Fun with u=λ x ≤ a.b :
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ a wf)₁ and (Γ,x ≤ a ⊢ b wf)₁.
Because x is a fresh variable, we can always alpha convert it to another name that does not exist already,
and as such the variable x is not used in Γ′ : no annotation of x exist in Γ′,
and all the annotations of Γ′ does not reference x.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ a wf)₁ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ a wf)₁.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ,x ≤ a ⊢ b wf)₁ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁,
we obtain (Γ,x ≤ a,Γ′ ⊢ b wf)₁.
Because x does not exist in Γ′, we have (Γ,Γ′,x ≤ a ⊢ b wf)₁.
By rule Wf-Fun, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ λ x ≤ a.b wf.
Rule Wf-App with u=a b :
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ a ≤*wf λ x ≤ w.⊤)₃ and (Γ ⊢ b ≤*wf w)₃.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ a ≤*wf λ x ≤ w.⊤)₃ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ a ≤*wf λ x ≤ w.⊤)₃.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ b ≤*wf w)₃ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u wf)₁,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ b ≤*wf w)₃.
By rule Wf-App, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ a b wf.
Suppose we are now in the case 2, that is (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂, let’s prove (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂.
We distinguish cases based on the last rule used in the derivation tree (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂.
Rule Ws-Rfl:
In this case, we have u=v=t.
By using the induction hypothesis on our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ t ≤wf t.
Rule Ws-Lf1:
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ v′◁_wft)₂,
(Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′)_i.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ v′◁_wft)₂ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v′◁_wft)₂.
By using Lemma 22
we obtain Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′
from Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≡ v′.
By rule Ws-Lf1, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v◁_wft.
Rule Ws-Lf2:
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ v′ ≤wf t)₂,
(Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′)_i, (Γ ⊢ v wf)₁ and (Γ ⊢ v′ wf)₁.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ v′ ≤wf t)₂ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v′ ≤wf t)₂.
By using the induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ v wf)₁ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v wf)₁.
By using the induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ v′ wf)₁ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v′ wf)₁.
By using Lemma 21,
we obtain Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′
from Γ;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′.
By rule Ws-Lf2, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v ≤wf t.
Rule Ws-Rgh:
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ v◁_wft′)₂,
(Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′)_i.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ v◁_wft′)₂ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u◁_wfv)₂,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v◁_wft′)₂.
By using Lemma 22, we obtain Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′.
By rule Ws-Rgh, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ v◁_wft.
Suppose we are now in the case 3, that is (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃, let’s prove (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃.
We distinguish cases based on the last rule used in the derivation tree (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃.
Rule Ws-Sub:
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂.
By using the induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤wf v)₂.
By rule Ws-Sub, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf v.
Rule Ws-Trs:
In this case, we have as premises (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf w)₃ and (Γ ⊢ w ≤*wf v)₃.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf w)₃ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf w)₃.
By induction hypothesis on the subtree (Γ ⊢ w ≤*wf v)₃ of our assumption (Γ ⊢ u ≤*wf v)₃,
we obtain (Γ,Γ′ ⊢ w ≤*wf v)₃.
By rule Ws-Trs, we obtain Γ,Γ′ ⊢ u ≤*wf v.

We distinguish based on the last rule used.

In this case, we have u=a b and v=a′ b with premise
By the induction hypothesis, we obtain Γ,Γ′;b::s ⊢ a ⟶≤ a′.

In this case, u=λ x ≤ t.a, v=λ x ≤ t.a′ and s=α::s₀

paper: Lemma 22 (Weakening of context - Equivalence reduction).
Let Γ;s and Γ′;s′ be two extended contexts such that Γ,Γ′;s@s′ is prevalid.
Let u and v be terms.
We have the following relations:
If Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v then Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
Proof.
By induction on the derivation tree of Γ;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
We distinguish based on the last rule used.
Rule Me-Var:
In this case, we have u=x and v=x.
By assumption, we have Γ,Γ′;s@s′ prevalid.
Hence by rule Me-Var, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ x ⟶≡ x.
Rule Me-Pro:
In this case, we have u=x and v=α′ with x ≡ α′∈Γ
and Γ;s ⊢ α ⟶≡ α′.
By induction, we have Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ α ⟶≡ α′.
Because x ≡ α∈Γ, we have x ≡ α∈Γ∪Γ′.
By assumption, we have Γ,Γ′;s@s′ prevalid.
Hence by rule Me-Pro, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ x ⟶≡ α′.
Rule Me-App:
In this case, we have u=a b and v=a′ b′ with premises
Γ;b::s ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and Γ;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
By the induction hypothesis, we obtain
Γ,Γ′;b::s@s′ ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and
Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
Hence, by rule Me-App, we conclude that
Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ a b ⟶≡ a′ b′.
Rule Me-Top:
In this case, we have Γ;s ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≡ ⊤ and
the derivation has no premises other than the prevalidity of the context.
By assumption, we know that Γ,Γ′;s@s′ is prevalid.
Hence, by rule Me-Top, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≡ ⊤.
Rule Me-Fun:
In this case, u=λ x ≤ a.b, v=λ x ≤ a′.b′ and s=nil
with premises Γ;nil ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and
Γ,x ≤ a;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
By the induction hypothesis we obtain
Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and
Γ,x ≤ a,Γ′;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
From the fact that x is fresh
(hence can be renamed so that it never appears in Γ′ ), we obtain
Γ,Γ′,x ≤ a;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
Therefore, by rule Me-Fun, we deduce that
Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ λ x ≤ a.b ⟶≡ λ x ≤ a′.b′.
Rule Me-FOp:
In this case, u=λ x ≤ a.b, v=λ x ≤ a′.b′ and s=α::s₀
with premises Γ;nil ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and
Γ;x ≡ α;s₀ ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
By the induction hypothesis we obtain
Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and
Γ,x ≡ α,Γ′;s₀@s′ ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
From the fact that x is fresh
(hence can be renamed so that it never appears in Γ′ ), we obtain
Γ,Γ′,x ≡ α;s₀@s′ ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.
Therefore, by rule Me-FOp, we deduce that
Γ,Γ′;α::s₀@s′ ⊢ λ x ≤ a.b ⟶≡ λ x ≤ a′.b′.
Rule Me-Bet:
In this case, u=(λ x ≤ a.b) c and v=b′[x c′]
with premises Γ;s ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′ and
Γ;nil ⊢ c ⟶≡ c′.
By the induction hypothesis we obtain
Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′ and
Γ,Γ′;nil ⊢ c ⟶≡ c′.
Therefore, by rule Me-Bet, we deduce that
Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ (λ x ≤ a.b) c ⟶≡ b′[x c′].
Rule Me-TAp:
In this case, u=⊤ b and v=⊤ with premise Γ;s prevalid.
By assumption, we know that Γ,Γ′;s@s′ is prevalid.
Hence, by rule Me-TAp, we obtain Γ,Γ′;s@s′ ⊢ ⊤ b ⟶≡ ⊤.

paper: Lemma 24 (Narrowing of context in subtyping reductions).
Let Γ;s be an extended context, let Γ′ be an additional context.
Let u, v, t and t′ be terms.
If Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v and Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′.
Assume that both u, v are well-formed in context Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′.
Assume also Γ ⊢ t′ wf.
Then there exists a term v′ such that we have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v′,
and Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;nil ⊢ v ⟶≤ v′,
and Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ v′ wf.
Proof.
If the derivation Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v
does not make a promotion of x to t, then we have
Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v
and v′=v satisfy the lemma.
Else, if the derivation Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ u ⟶≤ v
make a promotion of x to t, then we have
Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;nil ⊢ Co[x]⟶≤ Co[t′] with
Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;nil ⊢ Co[t′]⟶≡ Co[t]
by weakening to adapt the context and obtain the last derivation from Γ;nil ⊢ t ⟶≡ t′.
We now need to show that v′ is well-formed in context Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′
by induction on the structure of v′.
Case v′=x :
A variable is well-formed by rule Wf-PrS or Wf-PrE.
Case v′=⊤ :
We have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ ⊤ wf by rule Wf-Top.
Case v′=λ y ≤ t″.w :
We have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ λ y ≤ t″.w wf
by rule Wf-Fun with premise Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′,y ≤ t″ ⊢ w wf.
By the induction hypothesis, we have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′,y ≤ t″ ⊢ w wf.
Case v′=a b :
Because v′ and u are the same term, except for a promotion of x to t in head position,
we know in our induction that u=a′ b′ with b′=b.
Because u is well-formed, we have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ a′ ≤*wf λ y ≤ w.⊤
and Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ b′ ≤*wf w.

Let u, v, t and t′ be terms.

We do an induction on the derivation tree of Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v.
We distinguish cases on the last rule used.

We have u=v=y some variable.
The derivation Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;s ⊢ u ⟶≡ v hence holds by rule Me-Var.
Rule Me-Pro:
We have u=y and v=α′ with y ≡ α∈Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′ and Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′ ⊢ α ⟶≡ α′.
By prevalidity of the context, we know that y≠ x, and as a result we have y ≡ α∈Γ,Γ′,
hence y ≡ α∈Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′.
By rule Me-Pro, we therefore have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′ ⊢ y ⟶≡ α′.
Rule Me-Top:
By assumption, we have
Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′ ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≡ ⊤ with premise
Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′ prevalid.

By rule Ms-Top, we have Γ,x ≤ t′,Γ′;s ⊢ ⊤ ⟶≡ ⊤.

We have Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;s ⊢ a b ⟶≡ a′ b′ with premises Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;b::s ⊢ a ⟶≡ a′ and Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ b ⟶≡ b′.

We have Γ,x ≤ t,Γ′;nil ⊢ λ y ≤ w.u ⟶≡ λ y ≤ w′.u′

Impossible by assumption.

If y≠ x, then u[x\α]=y and v[x\α]=y.

paper: Lemma 33 (Congruence of ≤ ).
Let Γ;s be an extended context, and let u, u′, v, t and α be terms
We have these six congruence relations:
If Γ;v::s ⊢ u ≤ u′, then Γ;s ⊢ u v ≤ u′ v.
If Γ;v::s ⊢ u ≤* u′, then Γ;s ⊢ u v ≤* u′ v.
If Γ,x ≤ t;nil ⊢ u ≤ u′ then Γ;nil ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ≤ λ x ≤ t.u′.
If Γ,x ≤ t;nil ⊢ u ≤* u′ then Γ;nil ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ≤* λ x ≤ t.u′.
If Γ,x ≡ α;s ⊢ u ≤ u′ then Γ;α::s ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ≤ λ x ≤ t.u′.
If Γ,x ≡ α;s ⊢ u ≤* u′ then Γ;α::s ⊢ λ x ≤ t.u ≤* λ x ≤ t.u′.
Proof.
We do the first case. Every other case is similar:
it lifts Lemmas 34 and 35.
Suppose we have Γ;v::s ⊢ u ≤ u′.
By definition of the subtype relation, we have a term t such that
Γ;v::s ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ t and Γ;v::s ⊢ u′ ⟶≤↠ t.
By Lemma 35, we have Γ;s ⊢ u v ⟶≡↠ t v
from Γ;v::s ⊢ u ⟶≡↠ t.
By Lemma 34, we have Γ;s ⊢ u′ v ⟶≤↠ t v
from Γ;v::s ⊢ u′ ⟶≤↠ t.
We then conclude by definition of the subtype relation with the intermediate term t v.

Let Γ;s be an extended context, and let u, u′, v and t be terms
We have these congruence relations:
If Γ;v::s ⊢ u ⟶≤↠ u′, then Γ;s ⊢ u v ⟶≤↠ u′ v.

If s=nil :
